slides.text: Go has no overloading: one name, one function in a package. A second `connect` is rejected as redeclared, whatever its parameters. A variant gets a different name.
slides.code:
func connect(host string) {}

func connect(host string, port int) {}

slides.text:
There are no default or optional parameters either: a call passes every argument. Code works around it with a value that means "not set", or with a struct of options.

The module ends with `init`, a function Go runs for you.
A function named `init`, with no parameters and no results, runs by itself before `main`. Calling it by hand does not compile. A package may declare several.

exercises.title: One name per variant
exercises.guide: Go rejects a second `connect`, so each variant gets its own name.

chunks.guide: The plain variant: a URL with no port.
The secure variant gets another name, not another `connect`.

notes.text: A second connect would not compile: name it apart.

exercises.title: Default inside the function
exercises.guide: No default parameters: every call passes every argument. Treat zero as not set.

chunks.guide: Replace a zero port with the fallback.

notes.text: Zero reads as not set, even if the caller meant it.

chunks.guide: Pass the 0 to get the fallback, then a real port.

exercises.title: Where do the inits run?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output. Each call prints one line.
exercises.explanation: `init` functions run before `main` wherever they sit in the file, in the order written. A package can have several, unlike any other name.
